item.title: Backtesting a Strategy
item.description:
Backtesting is the process of simulating a trading strategy on historical data to evaluate its performance. Done carefully, it provides a useful signal about whether a strategy has merit — done carelessly, it produces misleading results.

The Basic Setup

A backtest requires three components: a signal (when to trade), a sizing rule (how much to trade), and a cost model (what execution costs). Getting all three right matters — an impressive backtest with no transaction costs tells you very little.

Common Pitfalls

The most dangerous backtesting mistakes are look-ahead bias (using future information that wouldn’t have been available at the time) and overfitting (tuning parameters until the in-sample performance looks good, at the expense of out-of-sample validity).

Evaluation Metrics

Raw return is a poor measure of strategy quality. Better metrics include the Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and the Calmar ratio — each capturing a different dimension of risk-adjusted performance.

References

Bailey, David H., Jonathan Borwein, Marcos Lopez de Prado, and Qiji Jim Zhu. 2014. “Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance.” Notices of the American Mathematical Society 61 (5): 458–71.
Sharpe, William F. 1966. “Mutual Fund Performance.” Journal of Business 39 (1): 119–38.

item.title: Volatility Targeting
item.description:
Volatility targeting is a position sizing technique that adjusts exposure inversely to realised volatility, keeping portfolio risk approximately constant through time.

The Core Idea

Rather than holding a fixed number of shares or a fixed notional position, a volatility-targeted strategy scales its position so that the expected portfolio volatility equals a target level :

where is an estimate of current volatility, typically a rolling standard deviation of recent returns.

Why It Works

Volatility is mean-reverting and persistent. When markets are calm, vol targeting increases exposure; when markets are turbulent, it reduces it. This creates a natural mechanism for cutting risk during drawdowns — often before stop-losses would trigger.

Practical Considerations

The choice of lookback window for matters significantly. Short windows are more responsive but noisier; long windows are more stable but lag regime changes. Transaction costs must also be weighed against the benefits of frequent rebalancing.

References

item.title: Put-Call Parity

Put-call parity is one of the most elegant results in options theory. It establishes a precise relationship between the prices of European calls and puts on the same underlying, with the same strike and expiration.

The Relationship

Deriving it from No-Arbitrage

The relationship follows directly from the no-arbitrage principle. Consider two portfolios: one holding a call and a bond, the other holding a put and the stock. Both portfolios have identical payoffs at expiration — so by no-arbitrage, they must have the same value today.

Implications

Put-call parity is model-free — it holds regardless of how we model the underlying. This makes it a powerful tool for detecting mispricing and for synthesising positions synthetically.

References

Hull, John C. 2018. Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives. 10th ed. Pearson.

item.title: Introduction to Options
item.description:
Options are among the most versatile instruments in modern finance. This post introduces the key concepts needed to understand how options work before we get into pricing theory.

What is an Option?

An option is a financial derivative that gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price on or before a given date. The price paid for this right is called the premium.

Calls and Puts

There are two fundamental types of options:

  • A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying at the strike price
  • A put option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price

Each can be either bought (long) or sold (short), giving four basic positions.

Key Terminology

Before diving into pricing, it helps to be precise about the core vocabulary: the strike price , the expiration date , the underlying price , and the risk-free rate . These four quantities appear in virtually every options model we will encounter.

References

Black, Fischer, and Myron Scholes. 1973. “The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities.” Journal of Political Economy 81 (3): 637–54.
Hull, John C. 2018. Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives. 10th ed. Pearson.
